contributions.headingText: Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) is a systemic histiocytic neoplasm characterized by multiorgan accumulation of mature histiocytes in a background of fibrosis.
2B31.Y & XH1VJ3 Other specified histiocytic or dendritic cell neoplasms & Erdheim–Chester disease
Not recommended: lipogranulomatosis; lipoid granulomatosis; lipid (cholesterol) granulomatosis; polyostotic sclerosing histiocytosis
ECD can affect virtually any organ system, including lung and pleura (see #14216) {24850756; 28553668; 29396850; 31472931}.

Patients mostly present with non-respiratory symptoms (see #14216). Lung involvement may be asymptomatic or may cause cough and/or progressive dyspnoea {28553668; 30154360; 20662053; 23396641; 31472931}. Pleural effusion and/or mediastinal infiltration is also common {31472931; 20662053}. Pulmonary function studies can show a restrictive pattern or may be normal. ECD can rarely be associated with Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Rosai–Dorfman disease, as well as autoimmune diseases {24894769; 26966089; 30923093; 31123032}. Myeloid neoplasms can be present in as many as 10% of cases {28679734; 31221777; 31624111; 31475353}.

Imaging

CT is helpful to demonstrate the pleural and/or parenchymal involvement, with reticulations and ground-glass opacities being the predominant parenchymal findings.

ECD is a rare disease. The age range is 15–80 years, with a male predominance (~70%) {24850756; 28553668; 29396850; 31472931}. ECD is extremely rare in children, in whom it is generally associated with Langerhans cell histiocytosis {19755920; 26466952; 30265230}.
ECD is a clonal neoplastic disorder {22879539; 26566875; 29192649}. Unlike in Langerhans cell histiocytosis, no association with cigarette smoking has been shown {29192649}.

Functional studies have shown that some cases derive from haematopoietic/myeloid progenitors {28566492; 28512190}. A characteristic cytokine signature responsible for local activation and recruitment of histiocytes has been identified {21205927; 29900045}. Gain-of-function alterations activating cell signalling pathways have been identified in nearly all cases {25150293; 22879539; 31768065; 26566875}.
The lung is firm, with pleural and interlobular septa often visible due to thickening.

Lung involvement has a characteristic lymphangitic distribution, along with involvement of the visceral pleura, interlobular septa, and perivascular interstitium as well as lesser involvement of the peribronchiolar areas. The disease typically spares perialveolar spaces {29192649}. The lesional histiocytes have foamy and/or eosinophilic cytoplasm, but they can be sparse and may have a distorted shape due to marked fibrosis admixed with chronic inflammatory cells. Eosinophils are rare to absent. Touton giant cells can be seen occasionally.

Immunohistochemistry

The lesional cells are positive for histiocytic markers (CD163, CD68, CD14, CD4, and factor XIIIa) and negative for CD1a and CD207 (langerin). S100 is variably positive. Immunostaining with BRAF p.V600E antibody (VE1) is not an optimal method to demonstrate BRAF p.V600E mutation in Erdheim–Chester disease {29192649}.
Bronchoalveolar lavage may show a nonspecific increase in histiocytes and/or chronic inflammatory cells {20662053}.
Demonstration of a corroborating genomic alteration may aid in diagnosis and treatment.

Most patients require systemic therapy. Traditionally, drugs such as peginterferon and cladribine have been used as initial treatments. However, in recent years, BRAF mutations have been recognized and tyrosine kinase inhibitors are used more frequently {29396850; 22300602; 24850756; 32187362}. Recent studies reported a 43–100% response rate and almost no disease progression with the use of BRAF and/or MEK inhibitors {30867592; 28667012; 29188284}. Prognosis depends on site and extent of the involvement. CNS involvement and multisystemic disease are poor prognostic factors {21239701}. Lung involvement is not an independent poor prognostic factor in recent case series {29396850; 20662053}.
